Transition Entropy Network

Source: R/transition_entropy.R
entropy_network.Rd

entropy_network() splits a chain's entropy rate into one term per transition and returns the terms as a network. The entropy rate \(h(P) = -\sum_{ij} \pi_i P_{ij} \log_b P_{ij}\) (transition_entropy(); Krejtz et al., 2015, 2025) is a sum over transitions, so every edge \(i \to j\) owns the exact term \(\pi_i P_{ij} \log_b(1/P_{ij})\) of the chain-level uncertainty. No new quantity is estimated: the network places the summands of the entropy-rate equation on the transition graph, which shows where in the process the uncertainty lies. Two other edge weights are available: each transition's surprisal, and its contribution to the entropy production rate (irreversibility). The result is a regular netobject, so it prints, summarises and plots (cograph::splot()) like any other Nestimate network.

Under the default weight, a heavy edge is a transition that is both frequent and unpredictable; under "surprisal", a heavy edge is a rare one, whatever its frequency. The weights are computed from one estimated transition matrix, so an edge that rests on a few observations can carry a large weight by chance: entropy_bayes() gives each contribution a credible interval and keeps only the edges that credibly hold a share of the entropy rate.

Usage

entropy_network(
  x,
  base = 2,
  weight = c("contribution", "surprisal", "production"),
  scaling = c("none", "share", "chance"),
  normalize = TRUE
)

Arguments

x

The chain: a netobject or cograph_network with non-negative transition weights, a tna model, a numeric transition matrix, or wide sequence data (a data frame or a character matrix, one row per sequence) that holds a numbered run of positions (T1, T2, ...), from which a relative transition network is built; other columns are set aside with a message. For a frame without such a run, build the network with build_network() (state_cols = or action =) and pass that. An association network (cor, pcor, glasso, ising, mgm) or a matrix with negative entries raises an error of class nestimate_not_markov. A netobject_group is not accepted; pass one network at a time.

base

The logarithm base, which sets the unit: 2 (default) for bits, exp(1) for nats, 10 for hartleys. Any positive number other than 1.

weight

What each edge's weight measures:

"contribution"

(default) \(\pi_i P_{ij} \log_b(1/P_{ij})\), the edge's additive share of the entropy rate; all edge weights sum exactly to \(h(P)\). Heavy edges are transitions that are both frequent and unpredictable.

"surprisal"

\(\log_b(1/P_{ij})\), the information content of observing the transition, ignoring how often it occurs. Heavy edges are rare, surprising transitions; a low surprisal marks an expected transition, which is the edge-level reading of predictability.

"production"

\(F_{ij} \log_b(F_{ij}/F_{ji})\) with \(F_{ij} = \pi_i P_{ij}\), the edge's contribution to the entropy production rate (irreversibility). It is positive on the dominant direction of a pair and negative on the reverse, and the two always sum to \((F_{ij}-F_{ji}) \log_b(F_{ij}/F_{ji}) \ge 0\). A pair with flow in one direction only has infinite production and is left out (weight 0); the number of such pairs is stored with the network's parameters. The total over the included pairs is the production rate. It is 0 for a reversible chain (detailed balance); when one-way pairs were left out, a total of 0 does not show reversibility, since such pairs mean the chain is not reversible.

scaling

How the weights are expressed. "none" (default) keeps them in base units. "share" (contribution only) gives each edge as a percentage of the entropy rate: the weights sum to 100, each one reads "this transition holds x% of the process's unpredictability", and they compare across networks whatever the number of states or the base. "chance" (surprisal only) divides by \(\log_b n\), the surprisal of a transition when all \(n\) next states are equally likely: 1 is chance level, below 1 an expected transition, above 1 one rarer than chance. "share" with another weight, or "chance" with another weight, raises an error.

normalize

Whether rows that do not sum to 1 (a frequency network, a count matrix) are divided by their sums, with a warning. With FALSE, such rows raise an error. Default TRUE. A state with no outgoing transitions (a row summing to zero) is an error either way.

Value

A netobject (class c("netobject", "cograph_network"); for a bare cograph_network input, that network with its own class) with method "entropy", whose weights are the per-edge entropy quantities. Print it for an overview; summary() (see build_network()) gives its network metrics, extract_edges() one row per edge, and cograph::splot() draws it. When x is a network (or sequence data, from which a relative network is built), the result is that network with the entropy weights swapped in: its initial probabilities, metadata, node groups and node coordinates are kept, so it plots with the same TNA styling and layout as its source. The stored parameters are base, weight, scaling, the entropy rate entropy_rate (whatever the weight) and the stationary distribution stationary, plus production_rate and n_oneway_pairs when weight = "production".

The object also declares the entropy house style through its meta$splot producer contract (honoured by cograph >= 2.4.4): no minimum-weight pruning (bit values are smaller than probabilities), edge labels with 2 digits (1 for "share"), vermilion edges, node rings showing the stationary distribution, and TNA rather than psychometric geometry. The production weights are signed, so they keep cograph's positive and negative edge colours instead of the vermilion. With weight = "surprisal" and scaling = "chance", the edges are drawn and sized by the transition probabilities, transitions likelier than chance in blues (darker for likelier) and those at or below chance dashed grey. Because the contract states the styling outright, cograph needs no knowledge of the "entropy" method: cograph::splot(ent) renders it with no arguments, and any argument given overrides the contract.

Details

An impossible transition (\(P_{ij} = 0\)) gets weight 0 under every definition (the \(0 \log 0 = 0\) convention), so the entropy network has no edge the transition network lacks. Self-loops are kept like any other edge; their production weight is always 0. A deterministic transition (\(P_{ij} = 1\)) also gets contribution and surprisal 0: observing the inevitable carries no information.

References

Cover, T.M. & Thomas, J.A. (2006). Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., chapter 4. Wiley.

Krejtz, K., Duchowski, A., Szmidt, T., Krejtz, I., Gonzalez Perilli, F., Pires, A., Vilaro, A., & Villalobos, N. (2015). Gaze transition entropy. ACM Transactions on Applied Perception, 13(1), 4:1-4:20. doi:10.1145/2834121

Krejtz, K., Hughes, C.J., Stasiak, I., Duchowski, A., & Krejtz, I. (2025). Real-time mobile transition matrix entropy based on eye and head movements. Proceedings of ETRA '25. doi:10.1145/3715669.3723128

See also

transition_entropy for the chain- and state-level summary, entropy_bayes for credible intervals on the decomposition, build_network.

Examples

net <- build_network(group_regulation_long,
                     method = "relative",
                     actor = "Actor", action = "Action", time = "Time")
ent <- entropy_network(net)
ent
